extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students or researchers interested in Australian comedy and humour
extracted.subtask_description: Describing the defining features, historical roots, formats, and notable strains of comedy performed in or about Australia and by Australians across media (literature, stage, radio, television, film, music, cartoons, festivals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Australian sense of humour (dry, irreverent, ironic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The "Australian sense of humour" is often characterised as dry, irreverent and ironic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: works and performers like Barry Humphries and Paul Hogan; character creations such as Norman Gunston and Roy and HG exemplify this tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laconic, ironic and irreverent wit (literary origins)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers like Henry Lawson and Banjo Paterson helped to establish a tradition of laconic, ironic and irreverent wit in Australian literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical grounding: bush balladeers and poets (e.g., C.J. Dennis) contributed to stoic, dry wit in vernacular writing such as 'The Loaded Dog' and 'Mulga Bill's Bicycle'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Larrikinism / anti-authoritarianism
rubrics_metrics.description: Vaudeville larrikinism and anti-authoritarianism are a hallmark strain (e.g., in the style of Graham Kennedy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roots in convict and colonial cultures and ANZAC dark humour; manifests as cheeky, irreverent attitudes toward authority in characters and performances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parochial satire and self-mockery
rubrics_metrics.description: Parochial satire and self-mockery are common strains in Australian comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The D-Generation, Roy & HG, Kath & Kim; self-mockery often targets suburban life and national quirks, with catchphrases entering the vernacular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sardonic political satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Sardonic political satire is a distinct and enduring strand of Australian comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Chaser, John Clarke and Bryan Dawe's mock-interviews, Rubbery Figures; frequently used to lampoon politicians and current affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and cultural commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy as social and cultural commentary delivered by broadcasters and writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners such as Clive James and Andrew Denton use comedic formats to critique society and culture; satire and commentary often coexist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiculturalism and diversity of perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiculturalism has contributed to a diversity in Australian comedy, with migrant and Indigenous voices prominent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: migrant comedians Mary Coustas, Anh Do; Aboriginal performers like Ernie Dingo; shows like Acropolis Now and Pizza use ethnic humour and multicultural settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Australian slang and vernacular
rubrics_metrics.description: Australian slang and vernacular are frequently used as a comedic resource.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples across songs, bush ballads and character comedy (e.g., Chad Morgan's country songs, novelty lyrics filled with local terms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character creation and impersonation
rubrics_metrics.description: Invented characters and impersonations are central techniques (e.g., Dame Edna, Sir Les Patterson, impersonations of public figures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Barry Humphries' characters, Gerry Connolly, Max Gillies, Billy Birmingham; character work used to satirise social vices and public personas and to 'encourage people to look at Australia critically and with affection and humour.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadpan, quirky, absurdist and dadaist delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Deadpan, quirky, absurdist and dadaist modes are notable delivery styles in Australian comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Elliot Goblet's deadpan stand-up; Barry Humphries' absurdist elements; these styles contribute to the distinctive 'dry' tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bawdy / blue humour strain
rubrics_metrics.description: A bawdy or 'bawdy' strain exists within Australian comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: comedians like Rodney Rude and Austen Tayshus; this covers risqué, explicit, or boundary-pushing material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty songs and musical comedy with Australian themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty songs and musical comedy that deploy Australian themes, puns and local references are a recurring form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Slim Dusty's 'Pub With No Beer', John Williamson's 'Old Man Emu', Rolf Harris's 'Tie Me Kangaroo Down Sport', The Twelfth Man's sports-parody singles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes and fish‑out‑of‑water comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy often exploits outback/bronzed-Aussie stereotypes and fish‑out‑of‑water contrasts for humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Crocodile Dundee (bushman-in-New York), films that contrast Australian archetypes with urban or foreign settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mockumentary and improvisational formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Mockumentary-style and improvisational formats are popular comedic forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Chris Lilley's mockumentary series, Thank God You're Here (improvisation), Russell Coight's All Aussie Adventures (mockumentary parody).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketch comedy as a dominant television form
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketch comedy has historically been a popular stalwart on Australian television, often preferred over the sitcom formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Mavis Bramston Show, The Naked Vicar Show, The Comedy Company, Fast Forward, Full Frontal; sketch shows frequently launched performers' careers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stand‑up comedy culture and festivals
rubrics_metrics.description: Live stand-up and festivals (notably the Melbourne International Comedy Festival) are central institutions for Australian comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MICF attracts large audiences and supports competitions like the Raw Comedy Award; stand-up performed at venues from pubs to major auditoria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television variety, panel and talk-show formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Variety, panel and talk-show formats have been important outlets for comedy and comic hosts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Graham Kennedy's In Melbourne Tonight, Hey Hey It's Saturday, Rove McManus, The Panel; these formats enable interviews, sketches, and talent showcases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radio as a longstanding comedic medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Radio has long provided a popular outlet for Australian comedy, from vaudeville-era performers to modern DJ duos and sketch segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Roy & HG, Merrick and Rosso, Martin/Molloy, Hamish & Andy; radio shows can incubate characters and reach national audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartoons and political cartooning as satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Cartoons (especially political cartoons) are integral to Australian political commentary and comedic practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical and contemporary practitioners: The Bulletin magazine's cartoons, Will Dyson, Pat Oliphant, Michael Leunig, Patrick Cook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards, festivals and competitions as recognition mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Festivals, awards and competitions (MICF, Raw Comedy, Bald Archy, Logies, AFI awards) function as measures of prominence and recognition in Australian comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Melbourne International Comedy Festival and associated prizes are important career milestones; Bald Archy parodies prize culture as part of comedic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy that critiques national identity with affection
rubrics_metrics.description: A strain of comedy aims to 'encourage people to look at Australia critically and with affection and humour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Barry Humphries' character work is presented as an exemplar: satire that is affectionate as well as critical, enabling reflection rather than merely derision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark humour rooted in wartime / ANZAC traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Dark humour and irreverence in the face of hardship are noted features, traced to ANZAC troops and wartime contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note: ANZAC troops displayed irreverence toward superiors and dark humour during conflict; this informs aspects of modern comedic sensibility.
